checks_performed: Read only the specified source input and draft; used no web access.
Compared the exact universal planar target against the draft's final writeup independently of claimed_resolution and self_assessment.
Rechecked all structural arguments, including disconnected and weighted reductions, tree-decomposition reasoning, cycle cases, and integer balance inequalities.
Ran check_explicit_examples.py using exact graph enumeration. It checked all 2,025 pairs of geodesics in K9 and the 15-vertex planar prescribed-three-geodesic obstruction.

Ran check_icosahedron.py using integer BFS and exhaustive enumeration. It certified the combinatorial sphere embedding, diameter 3, all 794 deletion sets of size at most four, all 162 geodesic vertex sets, and the explicit balanced two-geodesic union.

claims.claim: It suffices to treat connected nonempty graphs.
claims.evidence: For a nonempty disconnected graph, if every component is already at most half the total order, deleting any chosen path vertices preserves balance. Otherwise there is a unique component H larger than half. Applying the connected result inside H leaves its pieces of size at most |H|/2<=|G|/2, while every other component has size below |G|/2. Paths within H remain geodesics in G because no path can leave and re-enter a component.
claims.search_method: Direct reduction proof, including the already-balanced and unique-large-component cases

claims.claim: Balancedness is monotone under enlarging the deleted set.
claims.evidence: For X contained in Y, every component of G-Y lies inside a component of G-X. Its cardinality, and likewise its weight under nonnegative vertex weights, cannot exceed that containing component's value.

claims.claim: In a connected graph, every set X of at most four vertices is contained in the union of two geodesics.
claims.evidence: Pair four specified vertices and take a shortest path for each pair. With three vertices, pair two and use a trivial path at the third, or join it to an already paired vertex. The cases of at most two vertices are immediate. Connectedness guarantees the required shortest paths.

claims.claim: Any graph having a half-balanced vertex separator of order at most four satisfies the two-geodesic conclusion; the same statement holds for arbitrary nonnegative vertex weights.
claims.evidence: In the connected case, two geodesics cover the separator and deleting their possibly larger union preserves balance. In a disconnected weighted graph, either every original component has weight at most half already, or there is a unique heavier component H. In the latter case, cover the at-most-four vertices of X∩H by two H-geodesics; components inside H retain the assumed global half bound, and every other original component already has weight at most half.
claims.search_method: Direct weighted reduction and monotonicity proof

claims.claim: Every nonnegatively weighted finite tree has a centroid node whose deletion leaves tree components of weight at most half the total.
claims.evidence: Orient an edge toward a side of weight greater than half, when one exists. Two such heavy sides cannot occur at one vertex. A finite tree has a sink under these orientations, and every component obtained by deleting that sink is an incident side not exceeding half the total weight. The argument also covers total weight zero.

claims.claim: Every vertex-weighted graph tree decomposition has a half-balanced bag.
claims.evidence: Assign each graph vertex's weight to one decomposition node containing it and choose a centroid t of that weighted tree. For a component K of G-B_t, every vertex's bag-subtree avoids t. Bag-subtrees of adjacent vertices intersect, so connectivity of K places all assigned nodes for K in one component R of T-t. Hence w(K) is at most the assigned weight in R, which the centroid bounds by half the total.
claims.search_method: Direct proof from the running-intersection and edge-cover axioms of tree decompositions

claims.claim: If a connected graph has a tree decomposition in which every bag is contained in the union of two geodesics of the original graph, then those geodesics yield a half-balanced separator for every nonnegative vertex weighting.
claims.evidence: Choose a half-balanced bag using the weighted-bag lemma and then its stipulated two-geodesic cover. The geodesic union contains the bag, so every component left after deleting the union lies in a component left after deleting the bag and retains the half-weight bound.
claims.search_method: Direct composition of the balanced-bag result with deletion monotonicity

claims.claim: Every graph of treewidth at most three satisfies the target, even with arbitrary nonnegative vertex weights; planarity is unnecessary.
claims.evidence: A width-three decomposition has bags of size at most four. In each connected component, every such bag is coverable by two original-graph geodesics, so the weighted balanced-bag argument applies. For a disconnected graph, it suffices to work in the unique component whose weight exceeds half, if one exists; otherwise the graph is already balanced.
claims.search_method: Direct treewidth argument with an independent disconnected weighted reduction

claims.claim: In particular, every outerplanar graph and every planar graph with a universal vertex satisfies the target.
claims.evidence: Every outerplanar graph has treewidth at most two, as seen by completing an outerplane embedding to a maximal outerplanar graph and using triangular-face bags. If v is universal in a planar graph, deleting v leaves an outerplanar embedding because all remaining vertices lie on the face created around v. Adding v to every width-two bag gives width at most three, so the preceding theorem applies.
claims.search_method: Direct verification through standard explicit tree decompositions

claims.claim: If the largest component of an n-vertex graph has order m<=floor(n/2)+4, then the target holds. Consequently every nonempty graph on at most eight vertices satisfies it.
claims.evidence: If m<=floor(n/2), the graph is already balanced. Otherwise delete d=m-floor(n/2)<=4 vertices from the unique oversized component. At most floor(n/2) vertices of that component remain, and every other component has order at most n-m<=floor(n/2). The deleted set is coverable by two geodesics within its component. For n<=8, m<=n<=floor(n/2)+4, so the hypothesis always holds.
claims.search_method: Direct integer inequality and component analysis

claims.claim: The preceding eight-vertex bound is sharp without planarity.
claims.evidence: In K9 every geodesic has one or two vertices, so two geodesics delete at most four vertices and leave a connected clique of at least five vertices, exceeding 9/2. The checker enumerated all 45 distinct geodesic vertex sets and all 2,025 ordered pairs of them, confirming that none balances K9.
claims.search_method: Direct clique proof plus exhaustive exact enumeration

claims.claim: A connected graph satisfies the target whenever it has a half-balanced five-vertex separator X for which G[X] contains an induced path a-b-c.
claims.evidence: Because ac is absent while ab and bc are edges, a-b-c is a length-two geodesic in G. A shortest path between the other two vertices of X supplies the second geodesic. Their union contains all of X, and enlargement of a balanced deleted set preserves balance.

claims.claim: A half-balanced isometric cycle is sufficient, regardless of its length.
claims.evidence: Partition the cyclic vertex order into two contiguous blocks differing in size by at most one. Each block induces a cycle arc of length at most floor(|C|/2). Isometry makes each such arc a shortest path in G, and the two arcs cover every cycle vertex. Deleting their union therefore preserves the cycle's assumed half-balance.
claims.search_method: Direct cyclic partition and distance proof

claims.claim: In a planar graph, the vertex set of every half-balanced 5-cycle is coverable by two geodesics. A half-balanced induced cycle of length six is also coverable in any graph.
claims.evidence: For a 5-cycle, if every consecutive two-edge arc had adjacent endpoints, the five cycle edges and all five distance-two chords would form a K5 subgraph, contradicting planarity. Thus one consecutive triple is a two-edge geodesic, while the two remaining consecutive vertices form an edge-geodesic. For an induced 6-cycle, split the cyclic order into two consecutive triples; each two-edge arc has nonadjacent endpoints and is therefore geodesic.
claims.search_method: Exhaustive chord-pattern argument for C5 and direct induced-cycle argument for C6

claims.claim: A balanced union of three specified geodesics need not have a balanced two-member subunion, even in a planar graph.
claims.evidence: For the stated family, n=3m+6. Deleting all three pendant-edge geodesics leaves three components of order m. Any prescribed pair leaves a component of order 2m+2, and 2(2m+2)>3m+6 exactly when m>2. The graph is a 6-cycle with leaves and hence planar. The checker instantiated m=3: triple-deletion component sizes were 3,3,3, while every prescribed pair left a largest component of size 8 in a 15-vertex graph; it also confirmed an alternative two-geodesic separator with largest component 7.
claims.search_method: Symbolic integer calculation plus exact check of the smallest witness m=3
claims.witness: The m=3 graph obtained from a-x-b-y-c-z-a by attaching two leaves to each of a,b,c and one leaf to each of x,y,z

claims.claim: There is an explicit 12-vertex planar graph I of diameter three that remains connected after deletion of any four vertices.
claims.evidence: The checker constructed exactly the stated 12 vertices and 30 edges. It verified 20 distinct triangular faces, two faces incident with every edge, a single cycle as every vertex link, and Euler characteristic 12-30+20=2; this is a combinatorial sphere embedding and certifies planarity. Integer BFS gave diameter 3. Exhaustion of all 794 deletion sets of sizes zero through four found the remaining graph connected every time.
claims.search_method: Exact combinatorial sphere certificate, integer BFS, and exhaustive subset enumeration
claims.witness: The graph I on N,S,u_0,...,u_4,l_0,...,l_4 with the six edge families specified in the draft

claims.claim: The planar graph I has no half-balanced separator formed by one geodesic.
claims.evidence: Diameter 3 limits every geodesic to at most four vertices. Deleting any such set leaves I connected, with at least 12-4=8 vertices, which exceeds the half-order bound 6. Independently, the checker enumerated all 162 distinct geodesic vertex sets and confirmed that every deletion leaves one component larger than six.
claims.search_method: Deduction from diameter and four-deletion connectivity, backed by exhaustive geodesic enumeration
claims.witness: Graph I itself, with all 162 geodesic vertex sets exhaustively rejected as balanced separators

claims.claim: Two geodesics do half-balance I, so the preceding result establishes genuine necessity of the second path rather than a counterexample to the target.
claims.evidence: The checker verified that u_3-N-u_0-l_0 and u_3-u_2-u_1-l_0 are both length-three paths and that their common endpoints have distance three. Their union has six vertices. Its deletion leaves exactly the connected set {S,u_4,l_1,l_2,l_3,l_4}, of order six, meeting the half-order bound. Together with claim 16, this proves that one path can fail where two succeed.
claims.search_method: Exact endpoint-distance, edge, union, and residual-component checks

target_evidence: The exact target asks for a proof or counterexample covering every finite simple unweighted planar graph. The draft proves material proper subclasses and sufficient conditions—most notably all graphs of treewidth at most three—and supplies valid obstruction examples showing that a prescribed three-path separator cannot simply be thinned and that one geodesic is insufficient. It neither handles arbitrary planar graphs of treewidth at least four nor supplies a planar counterexample; graph I is explicitly balanced by two geodesics. The final writeup clearly states that the global question remains unresolved. Therefore the work is correct but incomplete progress, and its claimed resolution PARTIAL is accurate.
